newsitem.title: USA: Melting snow forms lakes in northern U.S. plains.
newsitem.headline: Melting snow forms lakes in northern U.S. plains.

text.p: Runoff from the melting winter snowpack pooled into vast lakes across the northern plains, pushing floodwaters into rural towns and forcing evacuations from isolated farmhouses, authorities said.
Dozens of towns and broad swathes of farmland were covered by icy waters as the spring melt inundated the fertile Red River Valley that divides North Dakota and Minnesota.

"The snow has been transformed into water and is turning vast areas into lakes, covering tens of square miles. It's flowing over fields, endangering rural communities and making its way to the Red River," North Dakota State University geologist Donald Schwert said in Fargo.
The city of 75,000 sits in the middle of the 50-mile (80 km) wide Red River Valley that extends like a geologic table-top into Canada.
Adding to the spring miseries was another storm that brought rain and heavy, wet snow to the hard-hit Dakotas and Minnesota.

"The rain and snow will only make things muddy, wet and sloppy and add to groundwater problems. The last thing people need is more snow," said Capt. Pat Richards of North Dakota's Division of Emergency Management.
No deaths or serious injuries had been reported since a woman and her teenage daughter died after plunging off a washed-out road with their horse trailer on Monday night.

Anxious officials in Fargo raised the anticipated flood crest of the adjacent Red River and moved massive pumps into position. Public works director Dennis Walaker asked residents to stay home from work to finish building dikes.
Backhoes and farm machinery were employed to break up ice and snowdrifts blocking culverts and ravines to divert floodwaters away from homes.

With the melting process moving gradually north, National Guard helicopters made repeated runs over the iced-over Red River, sprinkling sand on the ice to try to speed up the melt and prevent ice-jams.

Several tributaries of the north-flowing Red River had already reached record crests, and overland flooding blocked highways and swamped small North Dakota towns such as Casselton, La Moure and Milnor. Dozens of people had to be evacuated, some by four-wheel-drive vehicles, others by boat.
"The conditions are bad enough the way they are. The river models at some locations will exceed record levels -- even without the rain," National Weather Service hydrologist Wendy Pearson said.
Meanwhile, U.S. Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater toured flood preparations in Devils Lake, North Dakota, a resort area 120 miles northwest of Fargo.

In South Dakota and Minnesota, residents battled runoff from the steadily melting snowpack, building dikes, stacking sandbags and piling up mounds of gravel. Free tetanus shots were offered to those working in contaminated floodwaters.
Along the swollen James River in the southeast corner of South Dakota, volunteers joined prison inmates in the effort to keep schools, businesses and homes from being overwhelmed.
